summary: The Palas began around 750, when the chiefs of Bengal chose Gopala as king to end years of anarchy. Dharmapala and Devapala made Bengal and Bihar the base of a great Buddhist empire that fought the Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas for Kannauj and built the monasteries of Vikramashila and Somapura. After losing the west and much of Bengal in the 10th century, the Palas revived under Mahipala I and Ramapala, but the Sena dynasty pushed them out of Bengal in the 1150s and their line faded by about 1162.
details: In the early 8th century Bengal had no strong ruler. Local chiefs fought one another, a state of chaos later remembered as matsya nyaya, the 'law of the fish', where the big fish eat the small. Around 750 the chiefs agreed to choose one of their number, Gopala, as king. He ended the disorder and founded the Pala dynasty, which would rule Bengal and Bihar for some four centuries. Gopala ruled until about 770–775, laying the foundation for his son's expansion.

Gopala's son Dharmapala wanted to control Kannauj, the leading city of the northern plains. So did the Pratiharas of western India and the Rashtrakutas of the Deccan. Around 785–790 the Pratihara king Vatsaraja sent an army into Bengal that defeated Dharmapala. Then the Rashtrakuta king Dhruva defeated Vatsaraja and beat Dharmapala in the Ganges–Yamuna Doab. Dhruva went back south in 790, however, and in the end the Pala king gained more than he had lost.

With his rivals gone, Dharmapala marched on Kannauj around 791, removed its king Indrayudha and installed his own nominee, Chakrayudha. His Khalimpur copper plate says the rulers of Bhoja, Matsya, Madra, Kuru, Yadu, Yavana, Avanti, Gandhara and Kira attended the ceremony and accepted it. These kings probably kept their own lands and only recognised Dharmapala as overlord, and the claim may be exaggerated. Still, for a time the Pala king was the most powerful ruler in northern India.

The Palas were great patrons of Buddhism. Dharmapala founded the monastery of Vikramashila, on the Ganges near Bhagalpur in Bihar, in the late 8th or early 9th century; it became one of the main centres of Buddhist learning in Asia. He also built the Somapura Mahavihara at Paharpur, in today's Bangladesh, the largest of the Pala-era monasteries and a World Heritage Site since 1985. Scholars from these monasteries, such as Atisha, later carried Pala Buddhism to Tibet.

Around 798–800 the Rashtrakuta king Govinda III invaded the north, and Dharmapala and his protégé at Kannauj submitted to him. After Govinda went home, the Pratihara king Nagabhata II attacked. He took Kannauj from Chakrayudha and then defeated Dharmapala's army near Munger, in Bihar. One account dates the battle to 816; a Rashtrakuta inscription of 812 already mentions the Pala defeat. Kannauj passed to the Pratiharas for good, and the Palas' western ambitions shrank back toward Bihar.

Dharmapala's son Devapala ruled for about forty years, from around 810–821 to 850–861 depending on the historian. His inscriptions claim wide conquests: the king of Pragjyotisha (Assam) submitted without a fight, the Utkalas of Odisha were crushed, and he defeated the 'Gurjaras', meaning the Pratihara king Bhoja I. Some of these claims are probably exaggerated, but his reign marked the greatest extent of Pala power. He also granted villages for a Nalanda monastery requested by the Sailendra king of Java.

Devapala's death around 850 left the Palas exposed. The Pratihara emperor Mihira Bhoja, ruling from Kannauj, defeated the new Pala king Narayanapala and pushed east into lands near Gorakhpur. Narayanapala ruled for a long time, until about 908, but the Palas were now on the defensive. The great conquests of Dharmapala and Devapala in the west were lost, and the Pratiharas became the leading power of the northern plains, with the Palas confined to Bihar and Bengal.

In the 10th century the Pala kingdom came under attack from Kamarupa (Assam) and the Chandelas of Bundelkhand. Amid these invasions a family calling itself Kamboja took power in northwestern and southwestern Bengal, around Gauda, Burdwan and Midnapore, probably under Gopala II or Vigrahapala II (c. 960–986). Its origins are disputed, and some historians think its founder was himself a Pala prince. Raids by the Chandela king Dhanga and the Chandra king Kalyanachandra added to the turmoil, and the Pala realm broke apart.

Mahipala I, who came to the throne around 988 (some scholars say 978), led a Pala revival. His Bangar charter says he won back nearly all of north and east Bengal 'after defeating the usurpers who had seized his ancestral kingdom', thought to mean the Kambojas, who had been weakened by Chandela and Chandra attacks. He held Bihar as well and, by some accounts, pushed the Pala frontier as far as Varanasi. For a few decades the Palas were again a major power.

The Chola emperor Rajendra I of south India sent a great army north along the east coast, through Odisha into Bengal, between about 1021 and 1023. It defeated several local rulers, including the last Kamboja king of Dandabhukti, and then Mahipala himself, carrying off booty such as elephants and treasure. The Cholas raided rather than conquered and soon went home, but the invasion hampered Mahipala's revival and showed how exposed Bengal was.

Mahipala II, who had imprisoned his younger brothers Shurapala and Ramapala, faced a revolt by the Kaivartas, a community of north Bengal led by their chief Divya. Around 1075 Divya killed Mahipala II and took Varendra, the Palas' heartland in north Bengal, which Kaivarta chiefs, later including Bhima, went on to rule as their own kingdom. The two brothers escaped and reigned in turn, Shurapala for two years and then Ramapala. The Palas now risked losing still more land to the rebels.

Ramapala became king around 1077. Lacking a strong army, he won over powerful local chiefs with offers of gold and land. His cousin Sivaraja crossed the Padma river and devastated Varendra; Ramapala followed, and in a pitched battle the Kaivarta leader Bhima was captured and later executed. Ramapala ruled from a new capital, Ramavati, and brought Kamarupa and Rarh under his control, though he lost Mithila. His court poet Sandhyakar Nandi celebrated him in the Ramacharitam. It was the last great age of the Palas.

After Ramapala's death in 1130 his successors Kumarapala, Gopala and Madanapala ruled a shrinking kingdom. One of Ramapala's allies, the Sena chief Vijaya Sena of Rarh in western Bengal, had won his independence and grew stronger. Pala records continue to Madanapala's eighth year, 1152–53, after which Vijaya Sena most probably defeated him and took the throne of Gauda. The Palas lost Bengal, the land where their dynasty began, and kept only parts of Bihar.

Madanapala, the last widely recognised Pala king, ruled until about 1162. After him, kings named Govindapala and Palapala ruled parts of the Gaya district of Bihar until about 1200, though their link to the imperial Palas is uncertain. The Sena king Ballala Sena is credited with finally defeating Govindapala. After four centuries the Pala dynasty, which had ruled Bengal and Bihar and spread Buddhist learning across Asia, came to an end.
